page: Google Cloud Platform t2d-standard-60 is a general-purpose server instance belonging to the t2d family. It features 60 vCPUs mapped to 60 physical cores of an AMD EPYC 7B13 processor, utilizing the x86_64 architecture. The CPU allocation is dedicated, with 1.0 thread per core. The instance is equipped with 240.0 GB of RAM, providing a balanced 4.0 GB of memory per core. It does not include local storage or integrated GPUs, and has zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark data shows top-tier multi-core CPU performance, with stress-ng multi-core results placing in the top 10%. Single-core performance is strong, ranking in the top 25% for stress-ng single-core tests. Memory bandwidth for small cached blocks is strong, though large block read and write bandwidths fall into the average category. Multi-threaded operations, such as bzip3 decompression, software compilation with clang, and ray tracing, consistently achieve strong performance ratings.

The server exhibits a clear performance tradeoff when handling large-scale workloads. While prompt processing for small and medium language models is strong, text generation for large 70B models is weak, falling into the bottom 25%. This indicates a limitation for heavy generative AI tasks without GPU acceleration. The instance is highly suited for multi-threaded general-purpose workloads, database operations, software compilation, and web serving.

It features 240.0 GB of system memory, yielding 4.0 GB of RAM per core, with no local storage or GPUs included. Performance benchmarks indicate top-tier multi-core CPU capabilities, ranking in the top 10% for multi-core stress-ng tests, alongside strong results in software compilation, database operations, and multi-threaded decompression. However, memory bandwidth for large uncached blocks remains average, and large-model text generation is weak, highlighting a tradeoff for heavy AI workloads. This instance is optimized for compute-intensive general-purpose applications, multi-threaded processing, and database workloads.
